While about 1,000 ft above ground level, the friend observed the Mooney at a very low altitude. He then witnessed the Mooney bank sharply to the right, which was followed by an abrupt left turn and sparks before the airplane impacted the ground. A witness, who was leaving a self-storage facility, observed the airplane travelling west towards the airport. The witness stated that the airplane was at a low altitude, similar to a crop duster, when it turned right, climbed and then flipped over and went straight down. The witness drove to the accident site and saw a postaccident fire. The airplane came to rest upright in a ditch that was between an asphalt street and an orchard. The airplane was on a heading of about 212° magnetic at an elevation of about 531 ft mean sea level (msl). The first point of probable impact (FPPI) was about 40 ft from the main wreckage, in the middle of the street where the propeller spinner was located and flattened. A debris path with shards of acrylic and small bits of sheet metal extended from the FPPI to the main wreckage. A postaccident fire destroyed most of the fuselage and wings. The empennage was also thermally damaged. The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examinations.
NTSB:20260523203043.s: The pilot of a Mooney M20J ferrying the aircraft after maintenance reported a cylinder running 100°F hotter than others before departing. The airplane subsequently banked sharply, flipped, and impacted the ground near Woodlake, California, resulting in the pilot's fatal injury and a postaccident fire.

NTSB:20260526203045.n: On May 25, 2026, about 1110 Hawaii-Aleutian Standard time, a Sling Aircraft LSA, N83PF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Kalaupapa, Hawaii Airport (LUP). The two pilots onboard sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The airplane was being operated by Pacific Fight Academy, a 14 CFR part 61 flight school based at Honolulu Airport (HNL), Honolulu, Hawaii. According to the private pilot, he and his pilot-rated passenger were on a cross-country flight to the Island of Molokai to build time. They flew along the coastline of Molokai and were approaching LUP, the engine began to run rough, white smoke entered the cockpit through the air vent and the engine appeared to be losing power. The pilot shut down the engine and maneuvered the airplane to line up with the runway. He felt they would not make the runway and initiated a right turn toward a nearby bay to avoid landing on the rocky coast. The airplane contacted the water and immediately became inverted; both pilots self-extricated. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing, fuselage, and rudder. The accident airplane was equipped with a 100-horsepower Rotax, 912 iS Sport series engine. During the National Transportation Safety Board investigator-in-charge's follow-up examination of the engine, the No. 2 cylinder exhaust valve stem was observed to be fractured from the valve spring retainer, the valve stem had fallen into the No. 2 combustion chamber, metal fragments were present in the valve covers on all cylinders. Figure 1 Fractured valve stem The engine was retained by the NTSB for further examination.
NTSB:20260526203045.s: A private pilot and passenger in a Sling LSA N83PF experienced engine failure near Kalaupapa Airport due to a fractured No. 2 cylinder exhaust valve stem. The pilot attempted a water landing to avoid rocky terrain, resulting in an inverted crash, substantial aircraft damage, and minor injuries to both occupants.

NTSB:20260526203046.n: The pilot reported that he had been conducting glider tow operations and the gliders were landing back to the same airport that he had departed from. After releasing a glider, he flew west of the airport to survey the landing area due to the high volume of activity on the ground at the airport. He determined that he would land to a grassy area adjacent to the runway. The pilot maneuvered the airplane for a short base-to-final approach and noted that his approach speed was approximately 5 to 10 mph faster than normal with full flaps extended. He touched down "fairly firm" in a tail-low wheel landing attitude. After the tailwheel contacted the ground, he applied full aft elevator and braking. The landing area was rougher than anticipated, which caused the airplane to bounce and become airborne. When the main landing gear settled back onto the ground, the tail rose rapidly. The pilot released the brakes and applied full aft elevator; however, the airplane continued to pitch forward and nosed over, coming to rest inverted. The fuselage, left wing, vertical stabilizer, and rudder sustained substantial damage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. He further reported that he should have remained clear of the traffic pattern until the distractions in the landing area were clear, and he also felt he rushed the approach while conducting his traffic pattern maneuvers.
NTSB:20260526203046.s: The pilot conducting glider tow operations landed on a rough grassy area adjacent to the runway, experiencing a firm touchdown that caused the aircraft to bounce and nose over inverted. The pilot attributed the accident to rushing the approach and landing in a distracted environment rather than mechanical failure.

NTSB:20260526203047.n: The pilot reported that he was approaching the traffic pattern at his destination airport. A pilot from another airplane announced they were taking off from the same runway as the intended landing. After takeoff, the other airplane entered the downwind leg ahead of the pilot. The pilot got distracted by the other airplane now ahead of him and forgot to complete the before landing checklist. He subsequently landed without extending the landing gear, resulting in substantial damage to the lower fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operations.
NTSB:20260526203047.s: A pilot approaching the traffic pattern became distracted by another aircraft taking off and entering downwind, causing him to forget the before landing checklist. He subsequently landed without extending the landing gear, resulting in substantial damage to the lower fuselage.

NTSB:20260526203048.n: The pilot reported that while turning from base to final for landing on a lake, the airplane encountered a strong downdraft. The airplane descended below the intended flight path and impacted the water with the left wing low. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot reported that he should have maintained a higher altitude and flown a wider base to final turn to provide a greater margin in the event of encountering a downdraft.
NTSB:20260526203048.s: The pilot encountered a strong downdraft while turning from base to final for a lake landing, causing the aircraft to descend and impact the water left-wing low. The pilot attributed the accident to insufficient altitude and a tight turn, noting no mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260526203050.n: On May 26, 2026, about 0810 central daylight time, an experimental Fokker DR1 airplane, N54517, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Frankston, Texas. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. A witness and friend of the pilot, who observed the entire accident flight, was standing near the middle of the runway as the pilot taxied to the west end of the runway to begin the takeoff roll. He stated that this was the pilot’s first flight in the airplane. The takeoff was normal, but the airplane did not appear to climb well, and the pilot made an early right turn toward south and entered the traffic pattern. The airplane continued on the downwind leg at a low altitude, about 400 ft agl or less. The airplane then made a low west to east pass over the runway, which was recorded on video by another witness. The airplane then slowly climbed out and made another low and slow turn toward the south. The airplane remained low enough that his view was obstructed by trees on the south side of the runway. The airplane reappeared very low over the trees headed west-northwest, pitched up slightly, stalled, and made about one and a half rotations before it impacted the runway and exploded. A nearby doorbell camera, about 350 ft south of the accident site, recorded the sound of the engine during the accident flight. During the first lap in the pattern, the engine was operating and there were no audible anomalies noted. A few seconds before the accident occurred, the engine was operating and there were no audible anomalies noted; however, immediately before the sound of the impact, the engine sound decreased significantly. Postaccident examination revealed that the airplane came to rest upright facing east and a postimpact fire consumed a majority of the fuselage and cockpit. The wings remained relatively intact with thermal and impact damage. The wing bracing wires remained intact with the hardware installed. The empennage remained intact and was distorted to the right. The aileron control cables remained attached to the aileron surfaces and were continuous to the control stick attachment hardware. The elevator control cables remained attached to the elevator surfaces on the tail and were continuous to the control stick attachment hardware. The rudder cables remained attached to the rudder surface and tailwheel and were continuous to the rudder pedals. The throttle and mixture levers were found full forward on the power quadrant. The mixture cable and attachment hardware remained attached to the lever. The mixture cable was continuous through the firewall and up to the throttle body where it was found separated. The throttle cable threaded rod end, which connected to the throttle lever clevis, was fractured. The throttle cable was continuous from the threaded rod, through the firewall, and remained attached to the throttle body. The throttle Bowden cable consisted of a twisted/stranded inner wire, and a spiral wrapped outer sheath and metal jackets. The throttle body injector (TBI) was separated from the engine and the throttle mount plate was separated and not located. However, there were remnants of melted aluminum under the plate’s attachment screws. The throttle slide was found in a fully closed position; the slide was difficult to move due to damage to the TBI case. The spray bar remained installed and was positioned such that the holes were pointing 90° from the air inlet. The external fuel regulator sustained thermal damage. The engine was separated from the engine mounts and was resting near the front of the airplane. The engine remained intact with thermal and impact damage. The cylinders were intact with no signs of cracking or other catastrophic damage. The propeller was pulled through multiple times with no signs of engine binding. Seven of the nine cylinders produced suction and compression during the engine rotation. The two remaining cylinders had open valves due to push rod damage. The accessories on the rear of the engine sustained thermal damage. One of the wooden propeller blades sustained impact damage and was shattered. The other blade remained attached to the propeller hub with minimal damage and significant thermal damage on the blade face.
NTSB:20260526203050.s: The pilot of an experimental Fokker DR1 was fatally injured when the aircraft stalled and impacted the runway during a low-altitude traffic pattern. Post-accident examination revealed a fractured throttle cable and a closed throttle slide, which likely caused a loss of power leading to the stall.

NTSB:20260526203051.n: The flight instructor, who was flying from the left seat, reported that during the initial hover, the helicopter's engine governor reference rpm indicated about 104%. To adjust the governor reference rpm, the instructor reached across to the right-seat collective-mounted governor INCR/DECR switch. As he contacted the switch, the instructor failed to maintain helicopter control, and the helicopter pitched nose up, moved aft, and descended. The flight crew reported that the helicopter contacted the ground, bounced, and began to spin out of control. Airport surveillance video showed the helicopter moving aft while descending before contacting the taxiway. The helicopter subsequently became airborne, rotated to the right, and impacted the ground. During the impact sequence, the tailboom and main rotor system separated from the helicopter. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260526203051.s: A flight instructor flying a helicopter from the left seat lost control during an initial hover while adjusting the governor reference rpm, causing the aircraft to pitch up, descend, and impact the taxiway. The helicopter subsequently spun, became airborne, and crashed again, resulting in the separation of the tailboom and main rotor system.

NTSB:20260526203054.n: On May 26, 2026, about 1347 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-25-235 airplane, N8656L, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Saratoga Springs, New York. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 glider aerotow flight. The airplane was conducting an aerotow of a Schleicher ASW27 glider, N321ER via the glider’s center of gravity tow hook at Saratoga County Airport (5B2), Saratoga Springs, NY. Surveillance video showed that shortly after liftoff, at an altitude of about 200 ft, the glider pitched up and climbed above the towplane, pulling the tail of the towplane up and pitching its nose down. The glider pilot reported that he made several attempts to release before successfully separating from the towplane. The towplane did not recover from the upset, and subsequently impacted the runway, and a postcrash fire ensued. The glider returned to the airport and landed uneventfully. The towplane impacted about 50 ft right of the runway centerline in a nose down attitude and came to rest about 1,000 ft from the departure end of the runway. The debris path was oriented on a 330° magnetic heading and was about 100 ft in length from the initial impact point to the main accident site. At the initial impact point, two gouges about 1/2- to 3/4-inch-deep were observed in the asphalt, consistent with a propeller strike. Adjacent to the propeller strikes marks were rows of paint transfer consistent with wing contact. Thermal damage to the asphalt extended from the initial impact point to the main wreckage, and about 1 acre of grass adjacent to the runway was burned. The majority of the airplane was consumed by postcrash fire. The main landing gear was impact separated from the fuselage and located along the wreckage path. All the flight control surfaces remained attached to their respective attach points. The flap control lever was positioned to the flaps retracted position. The left aileron drive cable was separated about 11-inches from the wing root, the cable ends exhibited a splayed, broomstrawed appearance, consistent with a tension overload separation. Flight control continuity was established from the cockpit to all the flight controls except where separations were noted consistent with tension overload. The tow rope release latch and associated cable were continuous from the cockpit to the tail mounted latch mechanism. The engine was partially separated from the airframe and exhibited impact and thermal damage. Engine control continuity was established from the cockpit to the engine. The carburetor and oil sump were partially consumed by fire. Thermal damage precluded field tests of the magnetos. Crankshaft and valvetrain continuity was established during hand rotation of the crankshaft, with compression and suction observed on all six-cylinders. A borescope examination revealed no anomalies within the cylinders. The two-bladed, aluminum, fixed-pitch propeller was impact separated from the engine. One blade exhibited longitudinal twisting, leading-edge gouges, and chordwise abrasion at its outboard area. The other blade was bent aft about 20° midspan. The spinner was crushed aft and exhibited torsional deformation. The tow rope was located about 25 ft before the initial impact point. It measured about 195 ft in length and was constructed of twisted polypropylene. The weak link and metal rings remained intact and thermal damage was noted at both ends of the rope. Functional testing in the field confirmed that the tow rope latch mechanisms on both the glider and towplane were operational. Both aircraft were retained for further examination. NTSB:20260526203054.s: During an aerotow departure at 200 feet, a Schleicher ASW27 glider climbed above the Piper PA-25-235 towplane, causing a nose-down upset that the pilot could not recover from. The towplane impacted the runway and burned, killing the pilot, while the glider pilot successfully released and landed safely.

NTSB:20260526203055.n: The pilot of the tailwheel equipped airplane reported that, during the landing roll, and prior to the tailwheel contacting the runway surface, a gust of wind moved the tail of the airplane to the right. The pilot attempted to correct with right rudder input, followed by alternating right and left rudder inputs. However, the airplane ground looped to the left, and the right main landing gear collapsed. During the ground loop, the right wing struck the ground, which resulted in substantial damage to the right wing and aileron. The pilot reported that, at the time of the accident, he was landing the airplane on runway 1 with a west-northwest wind at 10 knots, gusting to 19 knots. According to the pilot, there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260526203055.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane ground looped left during the landing roll on Runway 1 due to a gusty west-northwest wind. The right main landing gear collapsed and the right wing struck the ground, causing substantial damage, with no preaccident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260527203056.n: On May 22, 2026, about 1518 eastern daylight time, a Textron Aviation 172S, N294PL, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Jupiter Farms, Florida. The flight instructor and student pilot were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The flight instructor reported that the airplane departed the North Palm Beach County General Aviation Airport (F45), West Palm Beach, Florida, with a total of 56 gallons of fuel onboard. About 40 minutes into the flight, while at an altitude of about 1,800 ft mean sea level (msl), during a practice climb, the flight instructor observed a decrease in engine rpm from 2,400 to 2,200. The flight instructor assumed control of the airplane; however, the engine rpm continued to decrease followed by a total loss of engine power. Unable to restart the engine, the flight instructor conducted an emergency landing in a plowed field, which resulted in substantial damage to the right wing. The airplane was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260527203056.s: During a Part 91 instructional flight in a Textron 172S, the flight instructor and student experienced a total engine power loss at 1,800 feet MSL while practicing a climb. The instructor executed an emergency landing in a plowed field, resulting in substantial damage to the right wing, though both occupants were uninjured.

NTSB:20260527203057.n: On May 23, 2026, about 1500 eastern daylight time, a Cessna A188B, N8288G, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Doerun, Georgia. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 agricultural flight. According to the pilot, during his fourth flight of the day the airplane sustained a total loss of engine power while en route to apply fertilizer to a corn field. The pilot initiated a forced landing to a field, during which the airplane struck trees before it came to rest upright, resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage and wings. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260527203057.s: The pilot of a Cessna A188B operating a Part 137 agricultural flight reported a total loss of engine power while en route to apply fertilizer. He executed a forced landing into a field, striking trees and sustaining substantial damage to the fuselage and wings, though he was not injured.

NTSB:20260527203061.n: The pilot reported that he executed a crosswind landing, crossing the runway threshold at an indicated airspeed of 95 knots. The airplane's main landing gear touched down at the 1,000 ft runway marker. During the landing roll, the pilot observed that the airspeed was increasing, and he realized the crosswind had shifted to a tailwind. He initiated a go-around because he believed that there was not enough useable runway to stop the airplane. The pilot stated that he attempted a soft-field performance takeoff during the go-around. However, the airplane was unable to climb out of ground effect and the airplane sank. The main landing gear impacted terrain beyond the runway surface and the nose landing gear collapsed. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mount. The reported wind at the time of the accident was 180 degrees at 11 knots with gusts to 15 knots. The crosswind component was between 10.8 and 14.7 knots. The pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operations.
NTSB:20260527203061.s: The pilot executed a crosswind landing in a 11-knot wind but initiated a go-around when a tailwind shift increased airspeed. The aircraft failed to climb out of ground effect, sank, and sustained substantial damage after the nose gear collapsed upon impacting terrain beyond the runway.

NTSB:20260527203062.n: On May 27, 2026, about 1130 central daylight time, a Cessna A188B airplane, N84497, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Blair, Nebraska. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, he flew the airplane from Millard Airport (MLE) in Omaha, Nebraska, to Blair Executive Airport (BTA) in Blair, Nebraska. When he landed the airplane at BTA, he was not satisfied with the landing, so he increased power after the airplane touched down on the runway to take off again. He reported that the airplane's engine had a reduction in power shortly after takeoff, and he landed the airplane in an adjacent field. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing. A postaccident examination revealed that the throttle cable was disconnected from the throttle body. A review of the airplane maintenance logbooks revealed that the throttle body was recently serviced. The airplane was recovered from the accident site, and it was transported to a secure location for future examination.
NTSB:20260527203062.s: The pilot of a Cessna A188B attempted a go-around at Blair Executive Airport after an unsatisfactory landing but experienced engine power loss due to a disconnected throttle cable. The aircraft was forced into an adjacent field, sustaining substantial left wing damage following recent throttle body maintenance.

NTSB:20260528203065.n: The flight crew of the business jet were approaching the destination airport near the conclusion of the transcontinental flight. The second-in-command (SIC) reported that air traffic control cleared the flight to land when the airplane was about 3 miles from the airport. Just after being cleared to land, the air traffic controller informed the flight crew that heavy rain would be encountered throughout the landing approach. The pilot-in-command (PIC) also described observing precipitation via weather radar and that a heavy rain cell had been reported on the runway. The SIC subsequently called the runway in sight when the airplane was about 250 feet above the airport elevation, and they continued the approach. As that airplane entered the landing flare, the forward visibility was extremely reduced, due to the heavy rain downpour, and the flight crew lost outside visual reference. Shortly after touching down the crew regained visual reference of the runway and realized that the airplane was drifting right of the runway centerline. The airplane continued right and the right main landing gear exited the paved runway surface into the grass. The pilots applied left control inputs, and the airplane rotated about 70° to the left before it came to rest on the runway, oriented nearly perpendicular to their approach path. The flight crew then applied power and were able to taxi to parking uneventfully. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing during the accident sequence. The PIC reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. A review of weather radar reflectivity data about the time of the accident showed that heavy to extreme precipitation was present on the approach to and over the airport. A special surface observation report was issued about the time of the accident and indicated ¾ statute mile of visibility in heavy rain, thunderstorms, and mist. Review of airport surveillance video confirmed that when the accident airplane was landing, the runway approach end was obscured by heavy rain, consistent with the flight crew, radar, and airport surface observation report. After the accident, the PIC stated, “We didn’t like the looks of the radar return, however there were no indications of sheer and the two aircraft ahead of us reported no issues. We flew a stabilized [instrument landing system] approach all the way to touchdown, but the visibility through heavy rain, gusty winds and wet runway condition should have been anticipated.”
NTSB:20260528203065.s: The business jet flight crew landed in heavy rain, lost visual reference, and veered off the runway, damaging the right wing. The pilot attributed the incident to unanticipated visibility loss from precipitation despite a stabilized approach and no mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260528203067.n: The pilot was on the final approach to the runway and reduced engine power too early resulting in a hard, bounced landing during which the nose landing gear collapsed, and the airplane nosed over. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the vertical stabilizer, rudder, both wings, and both wing struts. The pilot stated to an FAA inspector that there were no mechanical issues with the airplane before the accident and that it was due to pilot error.
NTSB:20260528203067.s: The pilot reduced engine power too early on final approach, causing a hard bounced landing where the nose gear collapsed and the aircraft nosed over. The pilot attributed the substantial damage to the vertical stabilizer, rudder, wings, and struts to pilot error rather than mechanical issues.

NTSB:20260528203068.n: The solo student pilot was conducting touch-and-go landings. He reported that during the landing flare, the airplane ballooned, and he was unable to maintain directional control. The airplane touched down and subsequently exited the runway, impacted a drainage ditch, and nosed over, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and rudder. The pilot reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260528203068.s: A solo student pilot lost directional control during the flare of a touch-and-go landing, causing the aircraft to balloon, exit the runway, and nose over into a drainage ditch. The pilot reported no mechanical malfunctions, and the accident resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and rudder.

NTSB:20260528203069.n: On May 27, 2026, about 1420 eastern daylight time, a special light sport Rainbow Cheetah XLS airplane, N146RC, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Knightdale, North Carolina. The flight instructor and student pilot were seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. The flight instructor reported that he was the pilot in command of the accident flight. He was conducting an introductory flight for a prospective student pilot and planned to demonstrate several maneuvers. The flight departed Cox Airport (NC81), Apex, North Carolina, with 15 gallons of fuel, destined for Raleigh East Airport (W17), Knightdale, North Carolina, for a low approach followed by touch-and-go landings. Upon arrival at W17 the flight instructor entered the airport traffic pattern, turned from the base leg to final approach, and aligned with the runway. He flew the airplane about 3 ft above the runway's surface and down its entire length before adding power to initiate a climb. As he added power, the engine began to "sputter" , so he reduced power and the engine stabilized and ran normal at a lower rpm setting. He added power again and the engine sputtered, so he reduced the power a second time. Realizing the airplane could not outclimb trees ahead, he turned right towards an open field. He attempted to add power several times; however, each time the engine would sputter. Unable to reach the field, he attempted to fly between a tree and a parked semi-trailer. The airplane struck the trailer and tree, fell about 30 ft and impacted the ground in a nose down attitude. The right wing separated from the fuselage, and the left wing's leading edge was damaged. The engine was displaced upward due to impact with the ground. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260528203069.s: A flight instructor and student pilot in a Rainbow Cheetah XLS suffered serious injuries when the aircraft struck a tree and semi-trailer during a low approach at Raleigh East Airport. The accident occurred after the engine repeatedly sputtered upon power application, preventing a climb over obstacles and forcing an unsuccessful attempt to land in an open field.

NTSB:20260529203073.n: The pilot-in-command was in the right front seat. She held a commercial pilot certificate and a current flight review endorsement. The passenger was in the left front seat. He held a student pilot certificate with a current 90-day solo endorsement and was flying the airplane during the accident takeoff. The airplane departed from a 3,000-foot-long grass airstrip with trees and powerlines off the departure end. The before takeoff checklist and engine run-up were completed without issue. The airplane used about 75% of the runway to become airborne. At that point, the student pilot (flying pilot) realized that the airplane was not going to clear the powerlines and trees. He turned the airplane to the left and "pulled back" on the flight control yoke. The airplane subsequently lost energy and impacted the ground near the departure end of the runway. Both pilots stated that there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures associated with the airplane before the accident. They noted that aborting the takeoff, once the airplane was not airborne at the halfway point down the runway, might have prevented the accident. According to the Airplane Owner's Manual, the estimated distance required to clear a 50-foot obstacle on a turf runway, under the accident conditions, was about 1,028 ft. The pilot's decision to continue the takeoff when the airplane was not airborne near midfield was the beginning of the accident sequence. In the absence of any airplane anomalies, it is likely that the flying pilot's handling technique resulted in the lack of sufficient climb performance, loss of control, and the impact with terrain.
NTSB:20260529203073.s: A student pilot flying a light aircraft from a grass airstrip continued takeoff past midfield despite insufficient climb performance. The pilot's decision to continue and subsequent control inputs caused the airplane to lose energy and impact terrain near the departure end.

NTSB:20260529203075.n: On May 22, 2026, about 1840 central daylight time, a Piper PA-32R-300 airplane, N4556Q, was substantially damaged during an accident near Comanche, Texas. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 business flight. The pilot reported that the airplane fuel system contained about 94 gallons of fuel before the flight and there were no issues with engine operation during a before takeoff engine runup. The pilot stated that the airplane was configured for takeoff with wing flaps at 25°, the fuel selector positioned to the left tank, and the auxiliary fuel pump turned on. The takeoff was conducted on runway 17. After an uneventful takeoff roll and liftoff, the pilot established a positive rate climb, retracted the landing gear, and retracted the wing flaps. The pilot was about to enter a left turn to west when the airplane had a sudden reduction in engine power. The pilot immediately turned left to enter a left traffic pattern for runway 17 as he verified that the engine throttle was full forward, the mixture control was full rich, the auxiliary fuel pump was on, and he selected the right fuel tank. The airplane was unable to maintain altitude and eventually there was a total loss of engine power. The pilot conducted a forced landing in a field on a heading of north. The pilot was able to extend the landing gear and wing flaps before landing in the field, but the airplane struck a barbed-wire fence and descended a hill. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings and the empennage during the accident. The airplane wreckage was recovered to a secure location where an examination will be conducted.
NTSB:20260529203075.s: The pilot of a Piper PA-32R-300 experienced sudden engine power loss shortly after takeoff near Comanche, Texas, likely due to fuel system issues despite switching tanks. The pilot executed a forced landing in a field, but the aircraft struck a fence and sustained substantial damage to the wings and empennage.

NTSB:20260529203076.n: The flight instructor stated that his student was practicing hovering in the helicopter. While hovering, the helicopter began to "slide down and to the left" . As the flight instructor gave verbal instructions to the student, the helicopter yawed to the right as the collective was pulled and moved to the left toward the ground. He said he remembered the left skid contacted the ground as he attempted to recover. The flight instructor believed that the skid caught on a crack in the pavement which resulted in the helicopter rolling to its left side. The student pilot reported that while hovering the helicopter started to "veer to the right" and the instructor said, "my controls" . Just at that moment the helicopter rolled onto its side. The operator reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation. In response to the accident, the operator instituted an internal review of hovering instruction methodologies, instructor intervention strategies, and low-hover risk mitigation procedures associated with primary and transition helicopter training. The organization implemented enhanced standardization measures focused on instructor recognition of early rollover precursors, intervention timing, verbal cuing techniques, and defined control transfer protocols during hover operations. Additional emphasis on dynamic rollover awareness, critical rollover angle recognition, and instructor decision-making during low altitude training events were also implemented.
NTSB:20260529203076.s: A flight instructor and student pilot were practicing helicopter hovering when the aircraft rolled onto its left side after the left skid caught on a pavement crack. The operator reported no mechanical failures and subsequently implemented enhanced training protocols for hover instruction and rollover risk mitigation.

NTSB:20260529203077.n: The pilot stated that he made an unstable approach, after which the airplane landed hard and bounced. A gust of wind caught the airplane's right wing during the bounce and the airplane veered off the left side of the runway. The left wing collided with a runway marker light and a directional sign, which resulted in substantial damage to the wing spar and punctured the fuel tank. The pilot was able to get the airplane back on the runway and aborted the landing. Once airborne, he smelled fuel, declared an emergency and landed without further incident. The pilot reported there were no mechanical issues that contributed to the accident and that he should have gone around versus trying to force a landing.
NTSB:20260529203077.s: The pilot executed an unstable approach, causing a hard landing and bounce that veered the aircraft off the runway into a light and sign, damaging the wing and puncturing the fuel tank. After aborting and declaring an emergency due to fuel fumes, the pilot landed safely, attributing the incident to forcing a landing instead of going around.

NTSB:20260529203078.n: On May 29, 2026, at 1138 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 172P, N96100, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Pembroke Pines, Florida. The flight instructor sustained serious injuries. The student pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. Prior to the accident flight, the airplane was flown 2.9 hours on a separate instructional flight. The student pilot then performed a preflight inspection of the airplane. The training plan for the flight was to practice flight maneuvers in preparation for solo flight operations. After discussing the training plan with the flight instructor, the student pilot retrieved the flight school-specific checklist and started the airplane’s engine. She then contacted air traffic control and was cleared to taxi to runway 28R at North Perry Airport (HWO), Pembroke Pines, Florida. Both pilots reported that an engine runup was conducted and that nothing abnormal was observed. The flight instructor then told the student to perform a short field takeoff. The student pilot then requested and was cleared for takeoff from runway 28R by air traffic control. During the takeoff, both pilots reported that the engine did not sound normal and that the flight instructor took control of the airplane. An airport operations employee reported that he observed the airplane at a low altitude and heard sputtering engine noises. A second witness also observed the airplane at a low altitude, then descending below trees. The second witness rushed to the accident site. The airplane was found inverted at the edge of a drainage pond, about 2,000 ft from the departure end of runway 28R. The witness then noticed a fuel leak in the engine compartment. To secure the airplane, he entered the cockpit, rotated the fuel selector to the off position, turned off the master switch and removed the ignition key. Post accident examination of the wreckage at the accident site by an FAA inspector revealed substantial damage to the airplane’s fuselage, empennage and wings. Fuel was found in both wings and the fuel strainer. The fuel was visually examined and no contaminants were observed. The engine oil dipstick showed 4.5 quarts of oil in the engine. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260529203078.s: A student pilot and flight instructor in a Cessna 172P suffered serious and minor injuries, respectively, when the aircraft crashed inverted near Pembroke Pines, Florida, during a short field takeoff. The accident occurred after the engine sounded abnormal and sputtered, causing a low-altitude descent and fuel leak, though no fuel contaminants were found.

NTSB:20260529203079.n: On May 28, 2026, about 1440 central daylight time, a Mustang Aeronautics Mustang II airplane, N160MT, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Richmond, Texas. The pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, he had recently purchased the experimental amateur-built airplane, and the airplane was based at the Covey Trails Airport (X09), Richmond, Texas. The airplane departed from X09 and was performing multiple touch-and-go landings to the single turf runway at the airport. While performing the multiple touch-and-go landings, the pilot reported he was utilizing the carburetor heat. During the final touch-and-go landing, just after the takeoff, the engine sustained a partial loss of power. The engine was unable to provide sufficient power to climb, and the pilot performed a forced landing. The airplane impacted a metal fence, and it came to rest upright on a flat grass field just to the south of X09 near a residential area. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and to both wings. The pilot reported that during the recovery of the airplane from the accident site, he drained about 10 gallons of 100 low lead fuel from the fuselage fuel tank (the sole fuel tank that has a 25-gallon useable capacity). The airplane was recovered from the accident site, and it was transported to a secure location for future examination. The airplane, which was built in 2007, was equipped with a Lycoming O-320-E2A reciprocating engine and a Sensenich Propeller Company 70CM6S16 two-blade fixed pitch aluminum propeller.
NTSB:20260529203079.s: The pilot of a Mustang II, N160MT, sustained minor injuries and the aircraft suffered substantial damage after a forced landing near Richmond, Texas. The accident occurred during a touch-and-go takeoff when the engine experienced a partial power loss while the pilot was using carburetor heat.

NTSB:20260529203080.n: The pilot reported that shortly after takeoff, the canopy opened on his experimental airplane because he failed to properly latch it before takeoff. He was unable to close the canopy after it opened and decided to land the airplane straight ahead on the remaining runway. The airplane subsequently overran the departure end of the runway and came to rest in the grass. The engine mount sustained substantial damaged. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260529203080.s: The pilot of an experimental airplane reported that the canopy opened shortly after takeoff due to improper latching. Unable to close it, he landed straight ahead, overran the runway, and sustained substantial engine mount damage with no pre-accident mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260529203081.n: The pilot reported that after touchdown the airplane swerved to the left, he over-corrected, and the plane swerved left again, so he applied power for a go-around. While airborne, the airplane was in a 10 to 15° right bank and the lower right wing impacted a runway sign. The airplane then impacted a grassy area on its right side and both right wings sustained substantial damage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260529203081.s: The pilot reported that after touchdown, the airplane swerved left, prompting an over-correction and a go-around. During the climb, the aircraft banked right, striking a runway sign and a grassy area, causing substantial damage to both right wings with no pre-accident mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260530203083.n: On May 29, 2026, about 2150 eastern daylight time, a Robinson R66 helicopter, N4488H, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Dawsonville, Georgia. The commercial pilot and one passenger were fatally injured. The other passenger had serious injuries. The flight was operated under the provision of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 as an on-demand air taxi flight. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) provided ADS-B data that showed the helicopter departed from a private wedding venue about 2145, and was enroute to DeKalb-Peachtree Airport, Atlanta, Georgia. The last recorded ADS-B point was at 2150:04, with the helicopter at 1,350 ft mean sea level (msl), travelling about 93 knots groundspeed (Figure 1). Figure 1. ADS-B with First Tree Strikes and Main Wreckage Annontated Impact signatures at the accident site were consistent with collision with tall trees and terrain in the Dawson Forest Wildlife Management Area. The first strikes were on tall trees along rising terrain following a general magnetic heading of 190°. Debris was scattered in a fan shape between 180-200°. From the first tree strike, the vertical stabilizer was located about 70 ft, the cockpit instrument panel at 173 ft, the main wreckage about 275 ft, the tail rotor gearbox at 297 ft, and the furtherest piece of wreckage, a portion of the main rotor blade was located at 472 ft. The main wreckage consisted of the pilots’ seat back, passenger cabin, main rotor mast, engine, and the beginning of the tailboom section. Portions of both main rotor blades remained attached to the main mast. The engine had fractured from the engine mounts but remained attached to the fuselage via fuel hoses (Figure 2). Figure 2. Wreckage Distribution The helicopter was recovered from the accident site and transported to a secure facility where additional documentation was performed. Examination of the airframe and engine did not detect any preimpact anomalies which would have contributed to the accident. A review of pilot information found that he completed his initial pilot testing and his line check on September 16, 2025, in both a Robinson R44 and a Robinson R66. He was graded satisfactory for all maneuvers. His pilot logbook was located at the accident site. He obtained his instrument helicopter rating on August 26, 2023, and received his commercial pilot certificate on November 10, 2023. The last entry was dated September 15, 2025. The closest aviation weather reporting facility was located about 13.8 miles to southwest of the accident site. At 2155, weather was reported to be 2 miles visibility with moderate rain and mist, and scattered clouds at 7,500 ft, with a remark for variable visibility from 1.5 miles to 3.5 miles. Modeling of weather near the accident site indicated the potential for light wind, a cloud ceiling near 200 ft above ground level (agl), and overcast clouds at 600 ft agl with rain and fog. A review of the National Weather Service (NWS) imagery showed the helicopter near an area of moderate rain at the time of the accident. Figure 3. Weather Image for 2150 with Accident Site Annotated The NWS also had a Convective Significant Meteorological Information (SIGMET) advisory issued at 2055 for an area of embedded thunderstorms moving from 220° at 15 knots with cloud tops near 40,000 ft. Figure 4. Convective SIGMET with Accident Site There was also Graphic Airman's Meteorological Information (AIRMET) advisories current for developing instrument flight rules conditions and mountain obscuration over the area. Figure 5. Graphic-AIRMETs
NTSB:20260530203083.s: A commercial pilot flying a Robinson R66 helicopter under Part 135 struck trees and terrain near Dawsonville, Georgia, while en route to DeKalb-Peachtree Airport in rain and low clouds. The accident caused substantial damage to the aircraft and resulted in the deaths of the pilot and one passenger, with no pre-impact mechanical anomalies found.

NTSB:20260531203085.n: On May 31, 2026, about 1236 central daylight time, a Pipistrel D O O Sinus 912, N1277P, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Columbus, Mississippi. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the airport manager from Columbus-Lowndes County Airport (UBS), Columbus, Mississippi, the pilot was observed arriving at the airport around noon. Airport security video showed the airplane takeoff a short time later. Preliminary ADS-B revealed that the airplane departed UBS about 1207 and flew in a northeasterly direction for about 15 minutes. The flight track indicated a turn to the west-southwest in a direction back toward UBS. ADS-B data ended about 8 miles northeast of UBS. Examination of the accident site revealed that the airplane was destroyed in a postcrash fire and came to rest upright adjacent to a field, near a rural residential area, about 5 miles northeast of UBS. The main wreckage came to rest on a magnetic heading of 148° at the base of a power transmission pole. The first identified point of contact (FIPC) was a power transmission line about 25 ft southwest of the transmission pole. All major structural components of the airplane were located at the accident site. The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260531203085.s: A pilot operating a Pipistrel Sinus 912, N1277P, was fatally injured when the aircraft struck a power transmission line and pole during a Part 91 personal flight near Columbus, Mississippi. The airplane was destroyed in a postcrash fire after departing Columbus-Lowndes County Airport and turning back toward the field.

NTSB:20260601203090.n: On May 30, 2026, about 0744 Atlantic standard time, a Cessna T210, N210PL, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Loiza, Puerto Rico. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that the accident flight was the first flight post maintenance. During takeoff and the initial climb, the engine was running normally with no discrepancies observed. After 5 minutes of flying, at about 3,000 ft mean sea level (msl), the pilot noticed an engine vibration. He then noted that after about 1 minute, the engine began to produce "explosion" noises, the oil pressure was very low, and the oil temperature was high. The pilot maneuvered to return to the departure airport and declared an emergency; however, the airplane would not have been able to reach the airport, and he performed a forced landing on a road. As the airplane touched down, it contacted a pole and quickly decelerated. Postaccident examination revealed that the airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing, fuselage, and empennage. An FAA inspector found several gallons of fuel in both fuel tanks. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260601203090.s: The pilot of a Cessna T210 experienced engine vibration, explosion noises, low oil pressure, and high oil temperature at 3,000 feet MSL during the first flight post-maintenance. Unable to return to the airport, he performed a forced landing on a road where the aircraft struck a pole, sustaining substantial damage to the wing, fuselage, and empennage.

NTSB:20260601203091.n: On May 29, 2026, about 1153 eastern daylight time, a Boeing E75, N181RF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Dresden, Ohio. The pilot and passenger were seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. A witness, who lived near the accident site with her husband, reported that she was standing in her yard and observed the accident airplane fly over her residence in a north direction. She then heard a loud "pop," and the engine noise ceased. The airplane subsequently impacted a hay field at her neighbor's residence across the street. Her husband ran to the wreckage to render assistance to the occupants. Initial examination of the wreckage by an FAA inspector revealed that it came to rest upright in the field, and both the upper and lower right wings sustained substantial damage. The wreckage was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260601203091.s: A pilot and passenger were seriously injured when their Part 91 Boeing E75, N181RF, crashed into a hay field near Dresden, Ohio. A witness reported hearing a loud pop and engine noise ceasing before impact, resulting in substantial damage to both right wings.

NTSB:20260601203092.n: On May 30, 2026, about 1113 central daylight time, a Grumman AA-1A airplane, N6416L, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Amery, Wisconsin. The pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight. The pilot reported that while en route on a positioning flight, he felt a sudden violent shaking of the airframe with a partial loss of engine power. He attempted to correct the power loss by applying carburetor heat, turning on the fuel pump, and switching fuel tanks; however, the shaking continued until the oil pressure decreased to zero followed by a total loss of engine power. The pilot established a best glide attitude and attempted to reach the nearest airport, which was Amery Municipal Airport in Amery, Wisconsin. While en route, the pilot realized he would not make the runway and chose to conduct a forced off-field landing into an open field about two nautical miles from the runway. During the off-field landing, both main landing gear collapsed which resulted in substantial damage to both wings. During recovery of the airplane, the engine was observed to have a hole in the crankcase next to the No. 4 cylinder. The airplane was retained for further examination.
NTSB:20260601203092.s: The pilot of a Grumman AA-1A experienced sudden shaking and total engine power loss during a Part 91 positioning flight near Amery, Wisconsin. After attempting an off-field landing, the main gear collapsed causing substantial wing damage, and a hole was later found in the engine crankcase.

NTSB:20260601203093.n: The student pilot reported that while practicing slow flight the airplane encountered "severe turbulence" during a turn and entered an aerodynamic stall/spin. Although he was able to recover from the spin, the airplane had insufficient altitude remaining to facilitate a full recovery to level flight before it impacted trees. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the wings and fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260601203093.s: A student pilot practicing slow flight encountered severe turbulence during a turn, causing an aerodynamic stall and spin. Although the pilot recovered from the spin, insufficient altitude prevented a return to level flight before the aircraft impacted trees, sustaining substantial damage with no reported mechanical failures.

NTSB:20260601203094.n: The student pilot was completing his third solo takeoff of the day. During the takeoff roll, he recognized that the flaps were still fully extended from the previous landing and subsequently moved the flap lever to retract them. The airplane veered left off the runway and struck two runway signs, then continued back onto the runway. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the elevator. The student pilot reported no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260601203094.s: A student pilot executing a solo takeoff retracted fully extended flaps during the roll, causing the aircraft to veer left, strike two runway signs, and sustain substantial elevator damage. The pilot reported no preimpact mechanical malfunctions.

NTSB:20260601203095.n: According to the pilot, while on final approach to the runway, the engine rpm began to run rough. The pilot applied carburetor heat, and the engine lost all power. The pilot attempted to restart the engine but was unsuccessful and prepared for a forced landing. The airplane touched down at the edge of a corn field and came to rest upright against a grass embankment. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing and fuselage. Following the accident, the pilot stated that the loss of engine power was likely the result of carburetor icing. According to the airplane handbook, during approach and landing, carburetor heat should be off unless icing conditions exist. The weather conditions at the time of the accident were conducive to the formation of serious icing at glide engine power settings.
NTSB:20260601203095.s: During final approach, the pilot applied carburetor heat in icing conditions, causing total engine power loss and a forced landing in a cornfield. The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the right wing and fuselage, with the pilot attributing the failure to carburetor icing.

NTSB:20260601203096.n: The purpose of the flight was for the solo student pilot to conduct takeoff and landing practice. The student pilot reported that during the soft-field landing, the airplane bounced and began to porpoise. As a result of the hard landing, the airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine firewall and lower fuselage. The student pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operations.
NTSB:20260601203096.s: A solo student pilot conducting soft-field landing practice experienced a bounce and porpoise, resulting in a hard landing. The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the engine firewall and lower fuselage, with no preimpact mechanical malfunctions reported.

NTSB:20260601203097.n: On January 22, 2026, about 18:40 eastern standard time, a Cessna 182T, N116D was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Newberry, Michigan. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight. The airplane departed from Saginaw County Airport (HYX), Saginaw, Michigan, about 17:15 on an instrument flight rules flight plan, flew northwest, and climbed to 10,000 ft mean sea level (msl). About 1 hour and 20 minutes after departing HYX, the pilot informed Minneapolis Center (ZMP) that the airplane was encountering " a little bit of ice" and requested a 30° heading change to avoid clouds. ADS-B data revealed that the airplane made a heading change of about 30° to the west-northwest. About 12 minutes later, the airplane began to descend in a spiral pattern from 10,000 ft msl. ZMP attempted to contact the pilot twice, but the pilot did not respond. About 1 minute after the airplane began the descent, the pilot told ZMP that the airplane was upside down and that he needed help. ZMP attempted to communicate with the pilot, but there was no response from him. About 2 minutes after the descent started, the pilot told ZMP that he was in control of the airplane and the airplane was level at 1,400 ft msl. ZMP asked the pilot to climb the airplane to 3,000 ft msl and gave him the option to land the airplane at Luce County Airport (ERY), Newberry, Michigan. The data showed that the airplane climbed to 3,000 ft msl and proceeded toward ERY. The pilot landed the airplane without further incident about 19:10 at ERY. A postaccident examination revealed substantial damage to both wings. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260601203097.s: A Cessna 182T pilot encountered ice and entered an uncontrolled spiral descent from 10,000 ft MSL near Newberry, Michigan, resulting in substantial wing damage. The pilot regained control at 1,400 ft MSL, climbed to 3,000 ft MSL, and landed safely at Luce County Airport with no injuries.

NTSB:20260601203098.n: The pilot reported that during landing the airplane ballooned and she executed a go-around. Before the airplane accelerated for the go-around it struck the ground hard and then became airborne again. The pilot said that during the second landing attempt a wind gust picked the airplane up and it hit the runway hard and began to porpoise. She believed that the airplane hit hard twice before she was able to get the airplane stopped. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. The airplane received substantial damage to the forward fuselage. The recorded wind at the accident airport were reported as 23 kts, gusting to 32 kts.
NTSB:20260601203098.s: The pilot reported that during landing in 23-knot winds gusting to 32 knots, the airplane ballooned, struck the ground hard, and porpoised on a second attempt due to a wind gust. No mechanical failures were reported, but the forward fuselage sustained substantial damage.

NTSB:20260601203101.n: The pilot reported that he and three club members assembled the glider before the accidewnt flight, following the manufacturer's assembly procedures. After a preflight inspection and positive control check, the glider was towed and released. Approximately 10 minutes later, the pilot heard a sharp cracking sound and elected to return to the airport and land. A postflight examination revealed substantial damage to the wing spar root, wing, and fuselage. During disassembly of the glider following the accident, the assembly crew noted that the right main wing pin was in its halfway position and had not been secured. The left main wing pin was fully inserted and secured. They noted that the in-flight structural damage was likely due to the right main wing pin not being fully seated and secured during assembly.
NTSB:20260601203101.s: The pilot and three club members assembled a glider before a towed flight. In-flight structural damage occurred because the right main wing pin was not fully seated and secured during assembly, despite the left pin being correct.

NTSB:20260602203102.n: On May 30, 2026, about 0900 Pacific daylight time, an Air Tractor AT-602, N5111A, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Robbins, California. The pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 Agricultural Aircraft Operations. The pilot reported that he was on an aerial seeding flight and that about 45 minutes after refueling he maneuvered toward a private airstrip to replenish his load. He added that the engine lost all power during a brief climb prior to landing at the airstrip when he was about 300 feet above ground level. After the pilot heard the engine spool down, the airplane started to sink. Subsequently, the pilot configured the airplane for best glide and executed a forced landing in a paddy field. The airplane nosed over shortly after touchdown and came to rest inverted, which resulted in substantial damage to the empennage. The airplane and engine were recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260602203102.s: The pilot of an Air Tractor AT-602 operating under Part 137 agricultural rules reported total engine power loss at 300 feet AGL while climbing to a private airstrip. He executed a forced landing in a paddy field, but the aircraft nosed over and inverted, causing substantial empennage damage and minor pilot injuries.

NTSB:20260602203103.n: The pilot reported that while in cruise flight at 1,500 ft mean sea level (msl), the engine lost power and the pilot observed a low fuel pressure indication. He engaged the manual fuel pump, and engine power was briefly restored. He turned the airplane back toward the departure airport, but the engine power remained unreliable. The pilot selected a highway for an emergency landing and landed as close to the right side of the westbound lane as practical to maintain separation from vehicular traffic. During the landing rollout, the right wing struck a road sign which pulled the airplane sharply to the right. The main landing gear collapsed, and the airplane came to rest in a ditch. The right wing sustained substantial damage. The airplane was examined after the accident. The fuel tanks were intact and no fuel was present. The pilot reported that he checked his fuel totalizer before the flight but was distracted by a conversation and did not verify the fuel quantity visually. He reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260602203103.s: The pilot experienced engine power loss at 1,500 ft MSL due to fuel exhaustion after failing to visually verify fuel quantity. He executed an emergency landing on a highway, but the right wing struck a road sign, causing gear collapse and substantial damage.

NTSB:20260602203105.n: The pilot reported that during his first landing attempt at the back-country airport, the airplane was too high on the approach, so he performed a go-around. He flew a longer final approach to prepare for the second landing attempt. After touchdown, the airplane was traveling too fast to stop before the end of the runway. The pilot said he "pulled up" to avoid vehicles parked at the departure end of the runway; however, the airplane did not attain sufficient altitude to clear the obstacles. The nose landing gear and lower fuselage struck an unoccupied parked vehicle, and the left wing subsequently struck a signpost. The airplane rotated about 180° and came to rest about 200 ft beyond the end of the runway. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. The pilot sustained a minor injury, and the passenger sustained a serious injury. The pilot further stated that he likely encountered a tailwind during the landing attempt. He noted that the density altitude and tight canyon operating environment were not familiar to him; that he did not verify the airplane's ground speed using the on-board GPS on the downwind and final legs. The pilot added that had he done so, he might have recognized the problem earlier. He stated that he had previously reviewed the Idaho Department of Aeronautics operating procedures document. Based on that information, he determined that once he had touched down on the runway he was committed to the landing, and a go-around was not advisable. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260602203105.s: The pilot landed a general aviation airplane at a back-country airport with a suspected tailwind and high ground speed, failing to stop before the runway end. He attempted to avoid parked vehicles by pulling up but struck a car and signpost, causing substantial damage and injuries due to unfamiliarity with the environment and lack of ground speed verification.

NTSB:20260602203106.n: On June 2, 2026, at 0945 eastern daylight time, a Cirrus SF50, N129KA, powered by a Williams International FJ33-5A turbofan engine, experienced an uncontained engine failure during climb from Greene County Regional Airport (KCPP), Greensboro, Georgia. There were no injuries to the pilot or passenger. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 general aviation flight from KCPP destined for Sgt. Lee Russell Carroll County Airport (KHZD), Huntingdon, Tennessee. According to the pilot, after takeoff at about 8,000ft above mean sea level (MSL), he received an engine inter-turbine temperature (ITT) warning and full authority digital engine control (FADEC) NO DISPATCH cockpit alerting system (CAS) message. He then contacted air traffic control (ATC) and requested a hold at 10,000 ft MSL, and in accordance with the checklist procedures, reduced the thrust lever setting by switching the auto throttle to manual mode and reduced the airspeed to 180 kts. The engine ITT temperature decreased, and the CAS message cleared. He reported that he remained at 10,000ft MSL for several minutes to monitor the engine parameters, and all remained within operating limits. The pilot then contacted ATC to request a small climb to see how the engine would perform, and after receiving authorization, initiated a climb to 13,000ft MSL. Seconds after advancing the engine throttle, there was a loud bang and reduction in power. The pilot reported that he pitched the airplane for best glide, declared an emergency, and received vectors to Athens-Ben Epps Airport (AHN), Athens, GA. While performing the emergency checklist procedure he attempted to “clear the engine,” which aggressively shook the airplane. He continued on vectors, deployed the flaps and landing gear, and made a no power landing on runway 9 at AHN. A post-incident examination of the airplane revealed an uncontained engine failure and separated section of engine cowl. A section of turbine disk protruded from the lower cowling structure on the right side of the airplane (Figure 1). Figure 1. Figure 1. Right Side of Airplane Engine, Post-Incident Inspection As part of the investigation process, the NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation, including the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Williams International, and Cirrus Aircraft. Party members from the FAA, Williams International, and Cirrus removed the engine at AHN and shipped it to Williams International in Pontiac, Michigan for teardown examination.
NTSB:20260602203106.s: A pilot flying a Cirrus SF50 experienced an uncontained engine failure during climb to 13,000 ft MSL after an initial ITT warning. The pilot declared an emergency and executed a no-power landing at Athens-Ben Epps Airport following a loud bang and power loss.

NTSB:20260602203107.n: The pilot conducted an aerial inspection of the grass runway before landing and observed no indications that the surface was unsuitable for operations. The landing was uneventful; however, during a subsequent turn to back taxi, the right main landing gear became stuck in soft terrain. After freeing the airplane, the pilot elected to use a soft-field takeoff technique to taxi the airplane to a drier portion of the runway. During this attempt, the nosewheel encountered another area of soft terrain, sank into the ground, and the propeller struck the ground. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the firewall and fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260602203107.s: The pilot landed on a grass runway, but the right main gear stuck in soft terrain during a back-taxi turn. While attempting to taxi to drier ground using soft-field techniques, the nosewheel sank, causing the propeller to strike the ground and damage the firewall and fuselage.

NTSB:20260602203108.n: The pilot landed the helicopter on an agricultural loading platform mounted on top a support truck to load spray material. After the loading operation was complete, the pilot signaled the ground crew member to stop pumping the spray material. The ground crewmember then approached the helicopter to speak with the pilot. After their brief conversation, the pilot initiated takeoff without verifying the loading hose had been disconnected from the helicopter's spray system. Upon realizing the hose remained attached, the pilot attempted to maintain a hover above the truck while the ground crewmember disconnected the hose. The ground crewmember was able to disconnect the hose; however, the pilot lost control of the helicopter, and it impacted terrain adjacent to the loading truck. The helicopter sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, cabin, main rotor system, and tail rotor system. The pilot reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
NTSB:20260602203108.s: The helicopter pilot took off from a loading truck with the spray hose still attached, causing a loss of control during a hover while the ground crew disconnected it. The aircraft impacted adjacent terrain, sustaining substantial damage to the fuselage, cabin, and rotor systems, with no pre-accident mechanical failures reported.

NTSB:20260602203109.n: The pilot of the tailwheel equipped airplane reported that during the normal landing, the airplane bounced and returned to the runway surface. When the landing gear contacted the runway surface, the airplane nosed over and sustained substantial damage to the rudder, vertical stabilizer, and left wing lift strut. The pilot was uncertain about his application of the brakes during the landing, however, the passenger reported that the airplane skidded after the main landing gear contacted the runway. Postaccident examination of the airplane identified wear marks on the main landing gear tires consistent with braking during the landing roll and revealed that there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot reported that the main landing gear wheels rotated freely when the airplane was towed from the runway. Based on the available information, it is likely that the pilot inadvertently applied excessive braking input during the landing roll.
NTSB:20260602203109.s: The pilot of a tailwheel airplane nosed over and sustained substantial damage during a normal landing after the aircraft bounced. The investigation concluded the accident was likely caused by the pilot inadvertently applying excessive braking during the landing roll.

NTSB:20260602203111.n: On June 2, 2026, at 0837 central daylight time, an AutoGyro Cavalon gyroplane, N113CX, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Coffeyville, Kansas. The pilot was not injured. The gyroplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, he was on his second solo flight of the day. During takeoff, about 10 to 30 ft above the runway, the gyroplane started to shake violently and roll to the left. The pilot attempted to correct the roll with full right cyclic and rudder but was unable to regain control. The gyroplane impacted terrain, bounced, and rolled several times across the ground before coming to rest on its left side resulting in substantial damage to the empennage, fuselage, and main rotors. The gyroplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.
NTSB:20260602203111.s: During takeoff of an AutoGyro Cavalon gyroplane on a solo Part 91 flight, the pilot reported violent shaking and an uncontrollable left roll at 10 to 30 feet. The aircraft impacted terrain, rolled, and sustained substantial damage to the empennage, fuselage, and main rotors, though the pilot was uninjured.

NTSB:20260603203113.n: On June 2, 2026, at 1151 eastern daylight time, a Piper J3C-65, N331JM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near East Granby, Connecticut. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot stated that after takeoff, when the airplane was about 400 ft, he noticed the engine rpm drop slightly. When the rpm continued to drop, he turned to return to the airport. As the airplane descended to about 200 ft, the engine lost all power. The pilot subsequently conducted a forced landing in a farm field. The airplane struck a greenhouse and the landing gear partially collapsed. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mount. The airplane was retained for examination.
NTSB:20260603203113.s: The pilot of a Piper J3C-65 experienced a total engine power loss at 200 feet after takeoff, forcing a landing in a farm field. The aircraft struck a greenhouse, causing partial landing gear collapse and substantial damage to the engine mount, though the pilot and passenger were uninjured.

NTSB:20260603203116.n: On June 3, 2026, about 1320 central daylight time, an Air Tractor AT-602 airplane, N50050, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Breaux Bridge, Louisiana. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 agricultural application flight. The pilot reported that the engine started normally and ran flawlessly for the initial portion of the 5-minute flight. The first indication of a problem was a short surge of engine power, followed shortly afterward by a second surge and an increase in engine temperature. The pilot retarded the power lever in response. Immediately afterward, the engine surged one more time with flames observed at the left exhaust. The engine then completely lost power and the pilot subsequently executed a forced landing to a field. The airplane remained upright with damage to the aft fuselage. Airframe and engine examinations are planned once the airplane is recovered from the accident site.
NTSB:20260603203116.s: The pilot of an Air Tractor AT-602 conducting an agricultural flight experienced engine surges, rising temperatures, and exhaust flames before total power loss. The pilot executed a forced landing to a field, resulting in substantial damage to the aft fuselage while sustaining no injuries.

NTSB:20260604203119.n: The flight instructor reported that the purpose of the flight was to reposition the airplane to a nearby airport to practice soft-field takeoffs and landings from a 2,000-ft-long, turf runway. During the repositioning flight, he reported that the wind was from the south-southwest at an estimated velocity of 4 knots. After landing on runway 5, the student performed an uneventful takeoff and landing on runway 23. The flight instructor then elected to back-taxi to runway 5 and demonstrate a soft-field takeoff. During the initial ground effect phase of the takeoff, the flight instructor observed an indicated airspeed of about 40 knots near midfield and that the airplane was not climbing. He then elected to reject the takeoff, and with insufficient runway remaining to stop, he reduced the engine power to idle, moved the mixture control to the idle cutoff position, applied the brakes, and maneuvered the airplane off the left side of the runway to avoid unsuitable terrain off the departure end of the runway. During the ground roll, the propeller impacted a roadway, and the lower fuselage of the airplane was substantially damaged. The flight instructor reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. At the time of the accident, the airplane was departing from runway 5. A weather reporting facility about 7 miles south of the accident airport reported that the wind was from 240° at 7 knots, which would have resulted in a tailwind during the takeoff. It is likely that the airplane's ground roll was increased as a result of this tailwind, which ultimately resulted in the flight instructor's decision to abort the takeoff and the subsequent runway excursion.
NTSB:20260604203119.s: A flight instructor aborted a soft-field takeoff on a 2,000-ft turf runway due to a tailwind preventing climb, causing a runway excursion. The aircraft struck a roadway with the propeller, sustaining substantial lower fuselage damage, with no mechanical failures reported.
